items.title: ‘Natural Realm Responded’: Filmmakers Detail Spiritual Manifestation on Set of New Movie
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

In Romans, the Apostle Paul wrote about the earth pointing to God’s “eternal power and divine nature.” The Koomans, two filmmaking brothers, certainly sensed that while making their newest movie, “Daniel and the Fiery Furnace.”

It unfolded when Mena Massoud, portraying Daniel, and Elijah Alexander, playing King Nebuchadnezzar, filmed a scene on-location in India from Daniel 2, when the king — furious over astrologers who couldn’t interpret his dream — ordered Daniel’s execution. Facing his would-be killers, Daniel visited Nebuchadnezzar, asking for more time to petition God for an answer to the king’s dream “so they would not be executed along with the other wise men of Babylon” (Daniel 2:18, NLT).

When Massoud began reciting his lines, telling Nebuchadnezzar the meaning of his dream, Daniel and Matthew Kooman told CBN’s “Faith in Culture” the atmosphere on set shifted powerfully.

The scene centered on the latter part of Daniel 2, when Daniel foreshadowed the coming of Christ and what many biblical scholars believe to be a reference to Jesus’ triumphant return in the end times:

During the reigns of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed or conquered. It will crush all these kingdoms into nothingness, and it will stand forever. That is the meaning of the rock cut from the mountain, though not by human hands, and crushed to pieces the statue of iron, bronze, clay, silver, and gold. The great God was showing the king what will happen in the future. The dream is true and its meaning is certain” (Daniel 2:44-45, NLT).

“[Massoud is] speaking these words from Scripture, and a wind blows across the set,” Daniel Kooman recalled. “Behind the camera, tents were hitting walls and blowing off set. A rainstorm, a crack of thunder — things that we hadn’t experienced in the natural realm on any day leading up to that for 25 days of prep and shooting. None of these sort of occurrences were happening until those words of Scripture about the everlasting kingdom that is coming [were spoken].”

“All of a sudden,” he said, “the natural realm responded to those words of prophetic Scripture.”

With an impressive $1.2 million raised in crowdfunding, the Koomans said they are confident audiences are eager for epic-style theatrical films like “Daniel and the Fiery Furnace.”

More importantly, Matthew Kooman told CBN News he is confident the project has divine backing.

“God was clearly behind it from the beginning,” he said. “And we were blown away by just the success of raising funds through people who wanted to be a part of telling the biblical story. That’s what the real synergy was.”

Trusting in the Lord — and standing by the courage of one’s convictions — is critical to success in Hollywood, the brothers said, particularly for filmmakers making content retelling biblical stories.

Calling the project “incredibly challenging,” Daniel Kooman said the one thing that kept him and his brother grounded was constant meditation on the source material, the Old Testament book of Daniel, and a genuine belief in the inerrancy of the totality of Scripture.

The movie pulls cross references from all throughout the Bible. In addition to Daniel, the film blends in scriptural accounts from the the books of Psalms, Isaiah, Habakkuk, and Jeremiah.

“We found practically … we couldn’t take one step on any given day without a leading or a direction from the Lord,” said Daniel Kooman. “That can sound abstract, but, for us, it was like, ‘OK, what are we gonna do today and how is it going to have an impact?’ It’s only gonna be if it honors the Word.”

Pointing to Isaiah 55:11, which says Scripture “always produces fruit” (NLT), Daniel Kooman said he noticed a one-to-one correlation that, when they dedicated themselves to accurately retelling the story of Daniel as it’s depicted in the Bible, “there was an incredible blessing.”

“People on set — actors and people involved in the production — experienced that,” he said. “It was a daily occurrence of God’s help through the production.”

Watch the full episode of “Faith in Culture” with the Kooman brothers in the video above.

items.title: MTV Star Leaves Gay Lifestyle After Encounter With Jesus
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Inspiring.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Davis Mallory was once an MTV star who lived an openly gay lifestyle while simultaneously adhering to what he called a Christian identity. 

Last year, though, “The Real World” star shocked fans when he shared a testimony during a Christian conference and it went viral. Then, earlier this month, he again found himself in the headlines after sharing images with his now-girlfriend. 

The initial reaction to his testimony was so intense last year that he said he faced death threats online in the wake of conservative and Christian activist Charlie Kirk’s murder.

This sparked a fair amount of fear in the reality TV star and singer — until God spoke through people and everything changed.

“I was singing in Hawaii and, on my flight home from Hawaii, I fell asleep on the plane, and I woke up, and all I heard was, ‘Lean not on your own understanding,’” Mallory said. “And I knew a little bit — that that was somewhere in the Bible, but didn’t know fully where it was. But I knew that God was saying, like, ‘I got you. You don’t understand what’s happening right now, Davis, but I got you.’” 

The next day, he had a dream where he was working with men in an Army bunker and he felt like God wanted him to be around other men of God. So, that night he went to a Bible study where he was prayed over. That same evening, a woman randomly approached him and said the Holy Spirit had prompted her to share a verse with him about fear. 

“She said, ‘I can tell you’re very afraid right now, and the devil wants you to stay afraid because you’ll make mistakes because you’ll trip,’” he recalled, noting that these events teamed with other messages from God finally brought him to a place of peace surrounding his story. 

This experience last year — and God’s provision — has enabled Mallory to speak out over the past few weeks and boldly share his journey to Jesus with total confidence.

“I have complete peace,” he said. 

The journey for Mallory has been a fascinating one, as his ascent on reality TV in many ways hinged on his formerly gay identity; today, it rests on Christ. 

“I … was thinking about the experience of being on a television show 200-plus years ago, making me famous for being gay, so to speak,” he said. “And the fact that I’m dating a girl today. If all of this was not on television, no one would know about it.“

Mallory, who grew up in a conservative and Christian household before initially coming out as gay, said there are many people going through similar circumstances in their personal lives, explaining that he believes God has used his journey and story to reach others. 

His journey is one that he’s openly reflecting on, explaining that he dated girls during his childhood before finding his affections turned toward men. Somehow, he said, being gay “overrid” his beliefs. But, over time, Mallory said everything transformed.

“For me, it was just gradual,” he said of his realization that homosexuality isn’t in line with God’s will. “It was failed relationship after failed relationship. It was falling in love with a man for him to then cheat on me with another man, and then to do it all over again, and all over again, and finding these relationships that were non-monogamous that were really lustful, and were really unfulfilling.”

Eventually, this mourning turned into questions. And when a Christian woman named Rachel came into Mallory’s life, he started digging deeper into faith — and questioning it all. When he attended a Christian conference and heard ex-porn star-turned-pastor Joshua Broome speak, something shifted.

“The fruits of my lifestyle was what was robbing me and it was actually Josh Broome and going to a Christian conference, hearing John 10:10 spoken where the devil comes to rob from you, to steal from you, and to kill you, and I thought about the homosexual lifestyle.” 

Mallory said he realized that the lifestyle was robbing peace from many around him, noting he had friends who had committed suicide and were unhappy; some even caught HIV. Others were simply unhappy that their expectations weren’t being met or found in same-sex relationships.

“I was just seeing that that lifestyle was really not producing the fruit of joy,” he said.

As Mallory’s friendship with Rachel grew, so did her spiritual influence. Over time, he started feeling an attraction to her and the two began dating — something that has transformed the MTV star’s life.

His relationship with Rachel has shown him a great deal about the true meaning of love.

“I was also seeing how lust will keep all of us attracted to every single person who’s beautiful because lust is just an attraction to beauty,” Mallory said. “But love is meeting the person that God designed for you.”

He continued, “And that was what I was finally feeling was this beautiful feeling of love, and I believe that every man, woman who has any kind of same-sex attraction can find this if they’re obedient and looking for it.”

Watch the rest of Mallory’s story above.

items.title: Singles Want Marriage More Than They Did 15 Years Ago
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: If marriage is supposedly dying, somebody forgot to tell single Americans. Indiana University’s Kinsey Institute has released new findings from its 15th annual Singles in America study, based on a survey of roughly 5,000 U.S. single adults. Forty-five percent said they’d like to get married someday.
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

If marriage is supposedly dying, somebody forgot to tell single Americans.

Indiana University’s Kinsey Institute has released new findings from its 15th annual Singles in America study, based on a survey of roughly 5,000 U.S. single adults. Forty-five percent said they’d like to get married someday. In 2010, it was just 33 percent.

The retreat from relationships has eased, too. The share of singles who said they don’t want a relationship at all peaked at 32 percent in 2021. It’s now 24 percent.

Marriage is getting more appealing. The timeline is getting longer.

Singles now say the ideal age to marry is later than it used to be, and they want to date longer before getting there. About 30 percent said they’d be open to a long-term committed relationship with no plans to marry.

They’re also getting more selective. Thirty-four percent now keep a checklist for a long-term partner, up from 25 percent in 2021. Half of Gen Z respondents said they research a date online before meeting them.

All that planning has its limits.

Nearly half of singles, 49 percent, said they’ve fallen for someone they weren’t initially attracted to, up from 30 percent in 2010. Great conversation was the most common reason attraction grew. Shared interests mattered, too.

“There’s an interesting tension in the data: singles today have clear expectations for a partner, but love still has the ability to surprise them,” said Dr. Justin Garcia, executive director of the Kinsey Institute. “Knowing what matters to you doesn’t mean knowing exactly who you’ll fall for.”

Singles are also becoming more flexible about some of the differences that once looked like obvious dealbreakers. Since 2019, the share willing to fall in love with someone with different religious views has climbed from 43 percent to 57 percent. Openness around differences on social issues and money rose as well.

Politics is messier. Political differences changed little overall, but party labels have become more likely to disqualify a potential partner, especially among Gen Z.

For all the filtering, the thing singles want most is pretty basic: someone they can trust and confide in. Thirty-nine percent selected it as one of their top priorities for a committed partner, followed by emotional maturity at 28 percent. About half of Gen Z and millennial singles said they want a partner who has been to therapy.

Money, meanwhile, is pulling in both directions.

More than half of singles, 52 percent, said the difficult economy has made them more interested in finding someone to share life with. In 2013, only 27 percent said the same.

At the same time, more singles say they need to be further along financially or professionally before getting serious with someone.

So, yes, dating now apparently involves checklists, online reconnaissance and possibly a therapist.

Marriage still gained 12 points.

items.title: A New Bible Study Opportunity for Evangelists
items.author: Nell O’Leary
items.summary:
Nell O’Leary

“It will be a beautiful biblical discussion extended through time and space: a microcosm of the Church’s own biblical life.”
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Nell O’Leary

The Word on Fire Institute is opening a new community group: the Bible for Evangelists Community. Enjoy this interview with the community’s leader, Vanessa Lopez, about the origins of the community, how it will function, and who it’s designed for.

* * *

Nell O’Leary: Vanessa, thank you for your time today to discuss the new community at the Word on Fire Institute: the Bible for Evangelists Community. This community launches on September 30, and we’re already hearing that people are very excited about a dedicated space at the Institute for this level of both guidance around Scripture and connection with others along the way. Please share with us a little about how this community came to be.

Vanessa Lopez: Nell, thank you so much for your help in getting the word out about this new community focused on the Word! Bishop Robert Barron says that “the Bible is the key to evangelization,” and equipping others to encounter the Bible well and share about the Bible well has always been at the heart of the mission of Word on Fire Catholic Ministries. Just look at the name of the ministry: proclaiming the “word” of God in and through the “fire” of God’s love, the Holy Spirit!

The Bible for Evangelists Community will launch on September 30, the memorial of the great biblical scholar and translator St. Jerome. Jerome famously said that “ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.” We want to know Jesus Christ more and help others come to know him.

September 30 is also the vigil of the memorial of St. Thérèse of Lisieux, the primary patron of Word on Fire. In fact, the Word on Fire Institute was launched on her day, October 1, back in 2018. Thus, the Bible for Evangelists Community will launch on the eve of the Institute’s eighth anniversary. I am delighting in how the number eight is evocative of eternity: seven days of creation followed by Jesus’s resurrection day, the “eighth day.” That is why baptismal fonts are often octagonal. Many members of the Word on Fire Institute have requested an opportunity to study the Bible together in a focused and systematic way, and it is a great joy to prepare this community in time for the Institute’s eighth anniversary.

You’ve been leading communities at the Word on Fire Institute since 2023, and I’ve had the pleasure of witnessing you in this role. You’re both a natural leader and filled with the curiosity of a life-long learner at the same time! How does this new role fit with your background and experience with Sacred Scripture? 

I have been reading, studying, and praying with the Bible since I was twelve years old. I had reached a milestone in the Protestant tradition of my childhood, and my mother gave me a “student Bible” as a gift. To her astonishment and delight, I actually read it! She had prepared me well for that moment by nurturing the seeds of faith, hope, and love planted in my infant baptism. 

I continued to read and study the Bible throughout high school, and when I reached college at Stanford University, I helped to lead Bible studies with my Christian fellowship group. I also naturally integrated Scripture into my literature studies. Eventually, it dawned on me that I wanted to study theology, and I enrolled in Fuller Theological Seminary in Pasadena, California, for a master’s degree in biblical studies and theology.

During my first term at Fuller, God put the finishing touches on the work of calling me into the Catholic Church. Learning about early Church history, including how the Bible came into existence, was a critical part of that call. How could Christians base their faith exclusively on the Bible if it was not fully assembled until the end of the fourth century? I came to see the need for the God-ordained teaching authority of the Catholic Church and to understand that the Bible is the Catholic Church’s book.

My biblical love and understanding have deepened considerably in my twenty-plus years as a Catholic. The Word of God is inexhaustible, so I am simply thrilled to get to continue my biblical formation together with my fellow Word on Fire Institute members.

Many of us are familiar with Bible stories, meaning we heard them when we were younger, and we hear them now as adults proclaimed at Holy Mass. But in recent years, we’ve seen enormous interest in being nourished by the Word. Examples that come to mind are Bishop Barron’s Sunday Sermons, free for anyone with an internet connection each Sunday, where he breaks open the Word with his signature humility and wit, or The Bible in a Year podcast with Fr. Mike Schmitz. In a world of perpetual content churn, this community offers systematic formation to become “biblically literate and biblically savvy evangelists” to use your description of it. What’s the format and flow of the community learning and sharing? 

It is an absolutely wonderful time for Catholics to be learning about the Bible. Thanks be to God for so many rich and complementary resources!

The Bible for Evangelists Community will follow a very straightforward format. We will be reading and discussing our way slowly through the volumes of the Word on Fire Bible (but people are more than welcome to participate with any Catholic Bible). We will therefore begin with the Gospels, and we will probably take two full years to go through them. We are most definitely aiming for depth rather than speed.

Once a week, I will make a group of posts that people can work through on their own time and at their own pace. There will be absolutely no pressure to “keep up” with anything, and people will be able to join the community at any point down the road and take themselves through the posts. It will be a beautiful biblical discussion extended through time and space: a microcosm of the Church’s own biblical life.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

We will also occasionally read and discuss resources from our great Catholic tradition, such as the Second Vatican Council’s Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, Dei Verbum, that will help us with biblical interpretation and application. And we will regularly welcome live guests to enrich our formation.

An essential aspect of this community is highlighted by the title: the Bible for Evangelists Community. We will consistently consider how to bring what we are learning into evangelization. The treasures of God’s Word must be shared! Also, people often have very misguided ideas about the Bible, and evangelists must be ready to help others “recover the depth and power of the Bible in the twenty-first century,” to quote Bishop Barron.

Holy Mother Church, in all her wisdom, has handed down teachings from the apostles to the early Church fathers all throughout the centuries to the holy popes and councils of our time. Your community will use the phenomenal Word on Fire Bibles for those who desire to purchase them (any Bible and Catholic translation will do!), which include teachings, writings, and explications of the Word. Would you explain how these “cathedrals in print” will be incorporative in the learning process of the community?

One of the primary purposes of the Bible for Evangelists Community is to accompany the Word on Fire Bible project, to offer readers of these extraordinary Bibles the opportunity to connect and discuss with others. That project was born out of Bishop Barron’s desire to draw people anew into the world of the Bible by leading with beauty and sharing the timeless treasures of Catholic biblical interpretation. Discussion posts will therefore be devoted to each essay and each artwork found in the Word on Fire Bible, as well as to each portion of Sacred Scripture. We will be extending the mission of the Word on Fire Bible by forming evangelists in the same ethos that informs every aspect of Word on Fire.

For those who feel like the Bible is very intimidating and that a community like the Bible for Evangelists Community must be restricted to folks with degrees in theology, would you please speak to how a new learner or someone early on in their faith journey could partake and benefit from the community and your leadership?

Just like the Word on Fire Bible, the Bible for Evangelists Community will welcome and benefit people of any and all levels of familiarity with the Bible. No previous biblical knowledge will be assumed, and people of all backgrounds will be encouraged to contribute their insights and experiences. The Word of God is for everyone!

Thank you so much for your time and the evident enthusiasm and servant’s heart with which you are approaching this new community. We will be praying for its success and for you as well!

items.title: Josef Pieper on the Four Cardinal Virtues
items.author: Dr. Tracey Rowland
items.summary:
Dr. Tracey Rowland

Pieper’s work on the cardinal virtues remains a treasure to be rediscovered by a new generation of Catholics seeking to understand the moral teaching of the Church as character formation.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Tracey Rowland

This article appears in Issue XXVIII: “The Cardinal Virtues” of the Word on Fire Institute’s quarterly journal, Evangelization & Culture.

Josef Pieper (1904–1997) was one of the biggest names in German Catholic life in the twentieth century. One of his many claims to fame is that he introduced Cardinal Karol Wojtyła (later St. John Paul II) to Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger (later Pope Benedict XVI). He was the catalyst for bringing them together. His action resulted in a quarter-century intellectual partnership, with Cardinal Ratzinger serving as St. John Paul II’s prefect for the Congregation of the Doctrine of the Faith from 1981 to 2005.

Pieper was also a Thomist philosopher famous for his books on virtue and tradition, including The Four Cardinal Virtues, published several times by different publishers, with its first English edition in 1954. In this book, he unpacked the meaning of prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, otherwise known as the “cardinal virtues,” first articulated in the works of Plato (the Republic) and Aristotle (the Nicomachean Ethics) and later adopted by Christian writers, including St. Ambrose and St. Thomas Aquinas. They are called “cardinal” virtues because the Latin word cardo means “hinge,” and they are the hinge upon which other virtues are hung.

Prudence: The Filter of Deliberation

For Pieper the meaning of the virtue of prudence is primarily this: “That not only the end of human action but also the means for its realization shall be in keeping with the truth of real things.” This in turn necessitates that “the egocentric ‘interests’ of man be silenced in order that he may perceive the truth of real things, and so that reality itself may guide him to the proper means for realizing his goal.” 

This idea of prudence has nothing in common with concepts like cunning or risk aversion. Rather, it is about having the capacity to read reality as it is and act upon this understanding. Pieper further explains that this requires the operation of what Aquinas called memoria, docilitas, and solertia. These three concepts are known as quasi-integral parts of the virtue of prudence.

With memoria, or memory, it is important that this faculty of the soul accurately recalls events as they were, that recollections are not falsified. With docilitas, there needs to be an openness to learning from others rather than an “I already know everything” attitude. Solertia is the capacity to take in various pieces of data and quickly conclude what the right, most prudential, action is, given the array of circumstances.

Pieper also explains that the cardinal virtue of prudence is assisted by the theological virtue of charity and the Holy Spirit’s gift of counsel. The theological virtues, the cardinal virtues, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit all play together in concert. The strength of the cardinal virtues is thus directly related to the strength of the theological virtues. 

Justice: The Habit of Giving Others Their Due

This second cardinal virtue is at the center of the Church’s social teaching. St. Thomas approached the subject by examining the relationship of individuals to one another, the relationship of the social whole to individuals, and the relationship of individuals to the social whole. These subclasses of justice are known as commutative justice, which orders the relation of individual to individual; distributive justice, which orders the relationship between the social whole to individuals; and legal or general justice, which orders the relationship of individuals to the social whole. Pieper explains that the hallmark of all three forms of justice is some kind of indebtedness.

The Church’s social teaching is critical of conceptions of justice that deny that the social whole owes anything to individuals or that individuals owe anything to the social whole. These mentalities are associated with the extremes of collectivism, typical of Communist and Fascist forms of government, and radical individualism, typical of libertarian forms of liberal political theory. 

Another central concept of Catholic social justice theory is the idea that it is the responsibility of governments to foster the common good (bonum commune). This is not very popular among liberal political theorists. They either deny that there is such a thing as a common good or offer a very narrowly defined version of it, on the grounds that individuals all have different conceptions of what, for them, is their good. John Rawls, one of the most celebrated liberal theorists of the twentieth century and a professor at Harvard University, said that if a man wanted to spend his life counting blades of grass, then that would be his good, and no one else had any standing to judge it otherwise. He also said that St. Thomas Aquinas was “irrational” and that St. Ignatius of Loyola was “mad.” 

Collectivist ideologies go in the opposite direction, promoting such an extensive view of what constitutes the common good that there is little or no respect paid to the legitimate freedom of individuals. Governments driven by collectivist ideologies will often use legislation to enforce social uniformity. In such countries, there is only one type of school, one curriculum, one healthcare system, one political party, and so on.

In addition to the above triad of relationships and their distinctive classes of justice, there is also the human person’s relationship to God. Pieper explains how St. Thomas Aquinas deals with the issue of justice in terms of the concepts of religion and piety. The latter is a disposition of the soul that recognizes a debt to its Creator which, of its very nature, cannot be fully repaid. Piety is also one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Fortitude: The Cardinal Virtue of Martyrs

Pieper begins his analysis of fortitude by remarking that angels cannot be brave because they are not vulnerable. Only those who are vulnerable, who have something to suffer, can be brave. He then defines the highest achievement of fortitude as martyrdom and describes the readiness for martyrdom as the essential root of all Christian fortitude.

Having begun on such a dramatic note, Pieper then assures his reader that fortitude has nothing to do with recklessness or a daredevil personality type. Rather, “genuine fortitude presupposes a correct evaluation of things, of the things that one risks as well as of those which one hopes to preserve or gain by the risk.” Fortitude therefore presupposes the operation of prudence and justice before it comes into play.

While Pieper’s treatment of the virtue of justice was strongly related to issues in contemporary political life, his treatment of fortitude veered into the territory of mysticism, linking the virtue to the concept of the dark night of the soul. Pieper quoted St. Teresa of Avila as saying that fortitude ranks first and foremost among the prerequisites for spiritual perfection. In her autobiography, she declared that “an imperfect human being needs more fortitude to pursue the way of perfection than suddenly to become a martyr.” Taking the first steps into the dark night and enduring the dark night require fortitude.

Fortitude is not only a cardinal virtue; it is also a gift of the Holy Spirit. As Pieper explained: “In the gift of fortitude the Holy Spirit pours into the soul a confidence that overcomes all fear: namely, that He will lead man to eternal life, which is the goal and purpose of all good actions, and the final deliverance from every kind of danger.” As such, “the supernatural fortitude bestowed by grace, which is the gift of the Holy Spirit, pervades and crowns all other ‘natural’ modes of Christian fortitude.” Pieper concluded this section by observing that those who go to war against various forms of social injustice without the fortitude of the mystical life are likely to fall victim to the “noisy sterility of spiritual pride.”

Temperance: Upholding an Ordered Whole

According to Pieper, temperance is about acting in such a way that the internal order of the person is fostered and upheld. It is linked to the forces of self-preservation, such as eating and drinking and reproducing. These powers can become violently self-destructive once they degenerate into selfishness and the virtue of temperance is not developed. What St. Thomas calls “the order of reason” must trump and restrain the temptation toward self-indulgence.

Pieper concluded that “to the virtue of temperance as the preserving and defending realization of man’s inner order, the gift of beauty is particularly co-ordinated. Not only is temperance beautiful in itself, it also renders men beautiful.” While this could be taken in a literal sense to mean that the person who is moderate in his intake of food and drink and who fasts on a regular basis is likely to be in better physical shape than someone less temperate, Pieper emphasized that he meant his statement to be taken as beauty in the spiritual sense, or what he called “the glow of the true and the good irradiating from every ordered state of being.” For Pieper, the ultimate meaning of temperance is linked to the purification of the senses.

Pieper’s work on the cardinal virtues remains a treasure to be rediscovered by a new generation of Catholics seeking to understand the moral teaching of the Church as character formation rather than duty parade rule following.
